questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Tangent
questions.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $25{x}^{2}=(5x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+25{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+(5x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(5x)}{5}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{9+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{9\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/9)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{9+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (3\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Secant
questions.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{|\sqrt{5}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{5}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{5}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{5}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{|\sqrt{5}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{5}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{5}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\sqrt{5}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{5}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{3}{\sqrt{3-75{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3\cdot (1-25{x}^{2})}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-25{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(5x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

  

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(5x)}^{2}.$   

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $-0.2$ | $0.2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-1$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{3}{\sqrt{3-75{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(5x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}\,\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(1)-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-1)) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}(\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\,\pi }{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.problem:
Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{12}{3+27{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}
$\operatorname{arctan}⁡($
{{field-2}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{12}{3+27{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=4{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{1+9{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $9{x}^{2}=(3x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $12$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{12}{3+27{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =4{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{1+(3x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{12}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{\int }_{0}^{12}\frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u{|}_{0}^{12} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(12)-\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\,arctan\,(12)\end{aligned}
$$
